title: The Cooling Effect of Plastic Clothes

paragraphs.text: The planet is not getting any cooler. In fact, some of the hottest years on record have occurred since 2010. It may be time to start thinking seriously about creating clothing more suitable for a warming world. That is what a team of researchers at Stanford University in the USA has been doing and, according to their published research, the clothes of the future could share something in common with the plastic goods we use on a regular basis.

The Stanford scientists are taking a close look at the cooling power of polyethylene, the most common plastic on Earth and the primary component of everyday plastic items such as bags, bottles and wrapping. They have discovered that a person wearing material incorporating polyethylene would definitely feel cooler than someone wearing cotton clothing. This is because of the way the material interacts with infrared radiation. Infrared radiation is basically the heat that our bodies produce. It is what makes us visible in the dark to someone wearing night-vision goggles. Roughly half our body heat goes out as infrared radiation. But if that radiation is trapped, we feel warmer. This is what normal clothes do - they trap infrared radiation. However, polyethylene does not: it has simple chemical bonds so the radiation can escape easily.

'The textile industry hasn't paid much attention to the infrared radiation property of clothing,' says Po-Chun Hsu, one of the Stanford researchers. It does not take a scientist, though, to recognize the disadvantages of using clear polyethylene as clothing. The obvious one is that it is transparent; that is, people can see through your clothes. But it also fails to absorb moisture, which could be problematic when people perspire. Where would the moisture go?

The Stanford researchers have been working hard to make polyethylene a more usable material. To address the issue of transparency, they found a version of polyethylene used to make batteries, one that is opaque to ordinary light but not to infrared radiation. So, while it is not transparent, it lets body heat pass through. As for the moisture problem, the scientists were able to use chemicals to modify the material, allowing water to spread across its surface, instead of forming droplets like it would on a rain jacket.

Scientists also inserted a layer of cotton mesh between two sheets of modified polyethylene to improve its structure. A sample of that mixed material and a small piece of regular cotton fabric were both placed on a surface with the same temperature as bare skin. Then a comparison was made of how much heat was trapped. The cotton fabric was found to make the surface two degrees Cel · warmer than the mixed fabric. Their aim is to create polyethylene clothing that feels 'more like clothes we wear'. Hsu says, 'We want to see if we can make it into more traditional cloth, with its softness.' To achieve this, polyethylene could be combined with more conventional fabrics, or it might be possible to actually make polyethylene into a woven textile.

Researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) are also analyzing the potential of using polyethylene as a way to make it easier for body heat to escape. But they're taking a somewhat different approach: 'We're working from the bottom up,' says researcher Svetlana Boriskina, who explains that the MIT team is working at the microscopic level, focusing on determining the right thiclmess of fibers necessary to make a fabric transparent to infrared radiation.

Boriskina's group is also working with polyethylene because of its unique properties when it comes to letting infrared radiation pass through it. Conventional fabrics, no matter how thin the fibers, will still capture sunlight and turn it into heat, but the plastic will not. 'Infrared light can escape it,' she says. The downside of polyethylene is comfort. Like if you touch it, does it feel good? This is the biggest challenge right now. And, how strong can you make it? If you put it through several washing cycles, I'm not sure it will survive.'

Despite polyethylene's disadvantages, Boriskina acknowledges that what the Stanford team has done is 'the first experimental demonstration that this idea does work'. While admitting that she may be overly optimistic, Boriskina thinks this type of clothing designed to keep people cool could be available in the near future. She pointed out that the clothing industry now works with rnicrofibers, so a process already exists. Manufacturers would need to do the same thing with polyethylene or another material that is infrared transparent.

How long this innovation will take to impact energy savings is another matter, Boriskina suggests. 'You would need to have a lot of people wearing this type of clothing. If too many people are still wearing conventional clothes, they may not want to turn down the air conditioner . 1
